items.title: 23.9 Hydrolysis of Acyl Chlorides, Alkyl Chlorides and Aryl Chlorides

source_refs.note: Topic 23.9 with Quick Check 23.5, answered (PDF 114-115); the equations are redrawn. The 14-day figure is the book's own; the Quick Check's peach and strawberry claim is not repeated. Exercises (PDF 115-117) are excluded. Answers need review.

blocks.text: The reactivity of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and aryl chlorides can be compared by how easily they are hydrolysed:

items: Ethanoyl chloride reacts rapidly with water at room temperature: CH3COCl + H2O -> CH3COOH + HCl. Its carbonyl carbon carries a large partial positive charge, because two highly electronegative atoms, oxygen and chlorine, are attached directly to it, so water attacks it so fast that the reaction is complete within minutes.

Chloroethane is hydrolysed only on heating under reflux: CH3CH2Cl + H2O -> CH3CH2OH + HCl. Its carbon is attached to only one electronegative atom, chlorine, so it is less positive and water attacks it much more slowly; the book says the reaction takes 14 days even at 100 C.

Chlorobenzene does not react with water. The carbon bonded to chlorine is part of the benzene ring, and a lone pair on chlorine is delocalised with the ring's pi electrons, giving the C-Cl bond some double-bond character; the bond is so strong that it does not break.

blocks.alt: Three panels. Ethanoyl chloride: CH3-C(=O)-Cl with a delta+ carbon carrying O and Cl; CH3COCl + H2O -> CH3COOH + HCl, fast at room temperature. Chloroethane: CH3CH2-Cl with a smaller delta+; CH3CH2Cl + H2O -> CH3CH2OH + HCl, slow, heat under reflux. Chlorobenzene: C6H5Cl; no reaction because the Cl lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
blocks.caption: Ease of hydrolysis of an acyl chloride, an alkyl chloride and an aryl chloride (original diagram after the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: The more positive the carbon attached to chlorine, the faster water attacks it. Ethanoyl chloride is the most reactive, chloroethane needs heating, and chlorobenzene does not react because its C-Cl bond is strengthened by delocalisation. Order of ease of hydrolysis: acyl chloride > alkyl chloride > aryl chloride.

blocks.prompt: Why do phenols not react directly with carboxylic acids to form phenyl esters?
blocks.explanation: A lone pair on phenol's oxygen is delocalised into the ring, so phenol is a poor nucleophile and does not react usefully with the weakly electrophilic carboxylic acid; a more reactive acyl chloride is used instead.

blocks.prompt: Write an equation for making phenyl ethanoate from ethanoyl chloride and phenol.
blocks.explanation: CH3COCl + C6H5OH -> CH3COOC6H5 + HCl (warm; a base such as NaOH helps by forming the phenoxide ion).

blocks.prompt: Predict the products: (i) chlorobenzene and ethanol; (ii) propanoyl chloride and phenol.
blocks.explanation: (i) No reaction: the C-Cl bond of chlorobenzene is too strong. (ii) CH3CH2COCl + C6H5OH -> CH3CH2COOC6H5 + HCl (phenyl propanoate).

items: Ethanoyl chloride: hydrolysed fast at room temperature (C attached to O and Cl).
Chloroethane: slow, needs reflux; chlorobenzene: no reaction (delocalised Cl lone pair).
Acyl chloride > alkyl chloride > aryl chloride.
